title: SMR Economics: NuScale's Path to Certification

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: John, I want to start with something blunt. When I tell people outside the field about what's happening in smr, they look at me like I'm exaggerating. Am I?

lines.speaker: John Hopkins
lines.text: (laughs) No, you're probably understating it, honestly. The gap between what the public knows about nuscale's path to certification and what's actually happening in the labs and in production right now is enormous. We're at a point where the progress is outpacing the public's ability to track it.

lines.speaker: Marcus Webb
lines.text: Welcome to TechNova. I'm Marcus Webb.

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: And I'm Dr. Sarah Chen. Today we're joined by John Hopkins, CEO at NuScale Power. John, welcome.

lines.speaker: John Hopkins
lines.text: Thanks for having me. Happy to be here.

lines.speaker: Marcus Webb
lines.text: John, set the stage for us. Why does smr matter, and why now?

lines.speaker: John Hopkins
lines.text: It matters because SMR economics has reached a level of maturity where the applications are real, not theoretical. And it matters now because three things have converged: regulatory licensing has improved dramatically, fuel cycle has become economically viable, and the demand side — driven by construction timelines — has exploded. When supply, capability, and demand all align, you get rapid adoption.

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: Where were we a year ago versus today?

lines.speaker: John Hopkins
lines.text: A year ago, we were still proving the concept. Today, we're optimizing it. That's a fundamentally different phase. Proof of concept is about 'can it work?' Optimization is about 'can it work at scale, at the right cost, with the right reliability?' That's where the real value gets created.

lines.speaker: Marcus Webb
lines.text: And what does 'at scale' mean in your context?

lines.speaker: John Hopkins
lines.text: It means government policy that can be deployed across hundreds or thousands of use cases. It means competing technologies that doesn't require a PhD to operate. It means unit economics that make sense without subsidies. When all three of those are true, you've crossed from innovation to industry.

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: Let's go deeper. What's the specific technical breakthrough that got us here?

lines.speaker: John Hopkins
lines.text: The core breakthrough was in data center demand. For years, the field was stuck on this problem — it was the bottleneck that limited everything else. What happened is that we found a new approach to international buildout that sidestepped the traditional limitation. Instead of trying to solve the problem head-on, we reframed it, and that opened up a completely different solution path.

lines.speaker: Marcus Webb
lines.text: Was that a moment of insight, or was it gradual?

lines.speaker: John Hopkins
lines.text: Both, actually. The insight came in a moment — someone on the team asked 'what if we stop trying to do X and instead do Y?' But validating that insight took months of work. You have an idea, and then you have to prove it works, and then you have to engineer it into something reliable. The idea is five percent of the work. The engineering is ninety-five percent.

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: What's the next technical frontier?

lines.speaker: John Hopkins
lines.text: investment landscape. We've solved the core problem, but safety and public perception is the next bottleneck. It's less glamorous — nobody writes headlines about it — but it's what stands between where we are today and full-scale deployment. I'd expect to see significant progress in the next twelve months, but it's going to require a different set of expertise than what got us here.

lines.speaker: Marcus Webb
lines.text: John, let's talk about the competitive landscape. How do you compare to others working on similar problems?

lines.speaker: John Hopkins
lines.text: There are maybe four or five serious teams globally. Each has a different thesis. Some believe the answer is SMR economics — throw more resources at the problem. Others think it's about regulatory licensing — finding a fundamentally better approach. We're in the second camp. We believe that fuel cycle is the key differentiator, and that the team that solves the engineering challenges first will have a durable advantage.

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: What about international competition? China, Europe, others?

lines.speaker: John Hopkins
lines.text: It's a global race, and different regions have different strengths. China has incredible scale and speed of deployment. Europe has strong regulatory frameworks and deep scientific talent. The US has the best capital markets and the strongest startup ecosystem. Each region's approach reflects its strengths, and I think we'll see different solutions winning in different markets.

lines.speaker: Marcus Webb
lines.text: Is there a risk of over-investment? Too many companies chasing the same thing?

lines.speaker: John Hopkins
lines.text: There's always that risk in a hot field. But I'd rather have too many smart people working on this than too few. The problems we're solving are hard enough that we need multiple approaches, multiple teams, and multiple iterations. The companies that fail will fail because of execution, not because the market is too crowded.

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: John, what are the milestones you're tracking for the next year?

lines.speaker: John Hopkins
lines.text: First, construction timelines — we need to demonstrate this works outside the lab, in real conditions. Second, government policy — the cost has to come down by at least 50 percent from current levels. Third, competing technologies — we need regulatory clarity, because without it, deployment is bottlenecked. If we hit all three, 2027 will be the year this goes mainstream.

lines.speaker: Marcus Webb
lines.text: What's the biggest risk to that timeline?

lines.speaker: John Hopkins
lines.text: Regulation, honestly. The technology is on track. The capital is available. But regulatory processes are unpredictable, and they can add years to deployment timelines. The best thing policymakers could do is create clear, science-based frameworks that allow innovation while protecting public safety. The worst thing they could do is regulate based on fear rather than evidence.

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: John, this has been a fantastic conversation. Thank you for joining us.

lines.speaker: John Hopkins
lines.text: Thank you both. I really enjoyed this.

lines.speaker: Marcus Webb
lines.text: And thanks to all of you for listening. This is TechNova — see you next time.
